subject: biology
prompt: You pull your hand away from a hot flame before you have time to think. Why is this response so quick?

options.text: The brain is able to think faster when there is danger
The nerves that detect heat connect to the nerves that move the muscle through a reflex arc in the spinal cord, so the signal need not wait for the thinking brain
The muscles of the hand decide on their own without any nerves
Pain receptors are present only inside muscles

image.alt: A hand touching a flame is pulled back instantly as a reflex action

hint: Where do the input nerve and the output nerve first meet?
explanation: A **reflex arc** joins the input (sensory) nerve and the output (motor) nerve at the point where they first meet, the **spinal cord**. The information still reaches the brain later, but the response does not wait for the slow, complicated thinking process. Muscles cannot act without a nerve impulse, and heat receptors are in the skin, not in muscles.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the part of the neuron where **information is first acquired** (first received).

image.alt: A neuron with branched dendrites, a cell body with nucleus, a long axon with myelin sheath and axon terminals while an impulse travels along it

hint: Information is detected at the tips of the branched fibres.
explanation: Information is acquired at the tip of the **dendrites**. It sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse, which travels from the dendrite to the cell body and then along the axon.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the part of the neuron where the electrical impulse is **converted into a chemical signal**. This signal is then passed on to the next cell.

image.alt: A neuron with branched dendrites, a cell body with nucleus, a long axon with myelin sheath and axon terminals while an impulse travels along it

hint: Think about the end of the long fibre that touches the next neuron.
explanation: At the **end of the axon** the impulse triggers the release of chemicals. These cross the **synapse** and start a new electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. The dendrite is where information is acquired, and the axon only conducts the impulse.

subject: biology
prompt: What happens at the **synapse** between two neurons?

options.text: The axon of one neuron fuses with the cell body of the next
An electrical impulse jumps across the gap as a spark
Chemicals released at the axon end cross the gap and start an electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron
The impulse stops and the signal is lost

image.alt: Two neurons at a synapse: chemical messengers leave the axon end, cross the gap and start an impulse in the next neuron's dendrite

hint: The gap is crossed by something other than electricity.
explanation: The electrical impulse reaching the axon end triggers the release of **chemicals**. They diffuse across the gap (synapse) and start a similar electrical impulse in the next neuron. The neurons do not fuse and the signal is not lost. A similar synapse passes impulses on to muscle or gland cells.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the steps by which a signal travels from one neuron to the next.

image.alt: Two neurons at a synapse: chemical messengers leave the axon end, cross the gap and start an impulse in the next neuron's dendrite

items.text: Impulse travels along the axon to its end
Dendrite tip detects information and a chemical reaction creates an electrical impulse
Chemicals are released and cross the synapse
Impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body
A new impulse starts in the dendrite of the next neuron

hint: Dendrite, cell body, axon, then across the gap.
explanation: Information starts at the **dendrite**, moves to the **cell body**, runs along the **axon**, and at the axon end chemicals cross the **synapse** to start a new impulse in the next neuron's dendrite.

subject: biology
prompt: You smell an agarbatti (incense stick). The smell is detected by **olfactory receptors** (smell receptors). Tap the sense organ that has these receptors.

image.alt: Side view of a head with the eye, ear, nose and tongue; scent particles drift towards the nose and sound waves towards the ear

hint: Olfactory means related to smell.
explanation: Receptors are specialised tips of nerve cells in sense organs. **Olfactory receptors** in the **nose** detect smell, **gustatory receptors** in the tongue detect taste. The impulse then travels along nerves to the brain, which interprets it as the smell of the agarbatti.

subject: biology
prompt: You pinch your nose shut and eat sugar. It tastes less sweet. What is the best reason for this?

options.text: The tongue stops working when the nose is blocked
Sugar does not dissolve in the mouth when the nose is blocked
Smell receptors in the nose also contribute to how food tastes, and they get no input when the nose is blocked
Taste buds only work when we breathe in

image.alt: A child pinches the nose shut while a sugar cube is eaten; the smell cannot reach the nose, so the taste seems weaker

hint: Think of what you notice when you have a cold.
explanation: Flavour combines **taste** (gustatory receptors on the tongue) and **smell** (olfactory receptors in the nose). With a blocked nose, such as during a cold, the smell input is missing, so food seems bland. The tongue and taste buds still work and sugar still dissolves.

subject: biology
prompt: One part of the brain is the **main thinking region**. It receives sensory impulses. It also has the centre that tells us we are full. This part is the

options.text: medulla
cerebellum
spinal cord
fore-brain

image.alt: Side view of the human brain showing the fore-brain, mid-brain, cerebellum, medulla and the start of the spinal cord

hint: Which of the three main regions is at the front?
explanation: The **fore-brain** is the main thinking part. It has areas for hearing, smell and sight, association areas that interpret information, motor areas for voluntary muscles, and a separate centre associated with hunger. The medulla and cerebellum belong to the hind-brain.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these belong to the **peripheral nervous system**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: The brain and spinal cord with cranial nerves and spinal nerves branching out to the body

options.text: Cranial nerves arising from the brain
Spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord
The brain
The spinal cord
Fore-brain

hint: The central nervous system is only brain plus spinal cord.
explanation: The **central nervous system** is the brain and spinal cord. The **peripheral nervous system** carries messages between the CNS and the rest of the body and consists of **cranial nerves** (from the brain) and **spinal nerves** (from the spinal cord).

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **cerebellum**. It keeps the body balanced and makes voluntary actions precise (exact).

image.alt: Side view of the human brain showing the fore-brain, mid-brain, cerebellum, medulla and the start of the spinal cord

hint: It sits at the back of the brain and has fine stripes.
explanation: The **cerebellum** (part of the hind-brain) controls the precision of voluntary actions such as walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle or picking up a pencil, and maintains posture and balance.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **medulla**. It controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.

image.alt: Side view of the human brain showing the fore-brain, mid-brain, cerebellum, medulla and the start of the spinal cord

hint: It is the lower part of the brain stem, just above the spinal cord.
explanation: The **medulla** in the hind-brain controls involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation and vomiting. The spinal cord below it is not part of the brain.

subject: biology
prompt: Which actions are **involuntary** and controlled by the medulla? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Side view of the human brain showing the fore-brain, mid-brain, cerebellum, medulla and the start of the spinal cord

options.text: Changes in blood pressure
Salivation
Vomiting
Writing a letter
Walking in a straight line

hint: Can you decide to do it by thinking?
explanation: The medulla controls involuntary actions: **blood pressure, salivation and vomiting**. Writing is a voluntary action planned by the fore-brain, and walking in a straight line needs the cerebellum for balance and precision.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each part of the nervous system with its function.

image.alt: Side view of the human brain showing the fore-brain, mid-brain, cerebellum, medulla and the start of the spinal cord

right.text: Precision of voluntary actions, posture and balance
Thinking, receiving sensory impulses and the hunger centre
Controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting

hint: Reflex arcs do not go through the thinking part of the brain.
explanation: The **fore-brain** thinks and has sensory and motor areas; the **medulla** controls involuntary actions; the **cerebellum** gives precision and balance; reflex arcs are formed in the **spinal cord**.

subject: biology
prompt: Which structure protects the **spinal cord**?

options.text: The vertebral column (backbone)
The skull
The fluid-filled balloon around the brain
The muscles of the arm

image.alt: The brain sits inside a bony skull and a fluid-filled balloon; the spinal cord runs inside the vertebral column

hint: Run your hand down your back to feel it.
explanation: The **vertebral column** protects the spinal cord. The brain is protected by the bony **skull** and the **fluid-filled balloon** inside it, which absorbs shocks.

subject: biology
prompt: How does a muscle cell **move** when a nerve impulse reaches it?

options.text: The cell absorbs water and swells without changing length
The cell grows longer by dividing
The cell moves along the nerve like a vehicle
Special proteins change their shape and arrangement so that the cell becomes shorter

image.alt: A nerve impulse reaches a muscle fibre and the muscle cell shortens as its proteins rearrange

hint: Animal muscle cells use proteins; plant cells use water.
explanation: Muscle cells have **special proteins** that change shape and arrangement in response to nerve impulses, giving a **shorter** cell. Plants, which have no muscle, instead change cell shape by changing water content.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the path of a **reflex action** when you touch a hot object.

image.alt: A reflex arc: heat receptor in the skin, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and muscle, with an impulse travelling along it

items.text: Impulse passes to a motor neuron in the spinal cord
Receptors in the skin detect heat
Motor neuron carries the impulse to the muscle
Sensory neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord
Muscle contracts and the hand is pulled away

hint: Input first, then spinal cord, then output.
explanation: The reflex arc runs: **receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord (connection), motor neuron, effector (muscle)**. The brain is informed too, but the action does not wait for it.

subject: biology
prompt: In a reflex arc, input nerves and output nerves are connected. Tap the part where this **reflex arc connection** is made.

image.alt: A reflex arc: heat receptor in the skin, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and muscle, with an impulse travelling along it

hint: Nerves from all over the body first meet in a bundle here.
explanation: Nerves from all over the body meet in a bundle in the **spinal cord**, so reflex arcs are formed there. The brain is not needed for the reflex itself.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the nerve cell that **carries the heat signal from the skin to the spinal cord**.

image.alt: A reflex arc: heat receptor in the skin, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and muscle, with an impulse travelling along it

hint: It carries input towards the centre.
explanation: The **sensory neuron** carries impulses from the receptor to the spinal cord. The **motor neuron** carries the output from the cord to the muscle (effector), and the receptor is only the sensing tip.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A reflex arc: heat receptor in the skin, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and muscle, with an impulse travelling along it

assertion: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord.
reason: Nerves from all over the body meet in a bundle in the spinal cord. This is where input and output nerves first meet.
hint: Think about the shortest connection between input and output.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. The spinal cord is where input and output nerves first meet, so the simplest connection (reflex arc) is formed there, giving a quick response.

subject: biology
prompt: A person has an injury that cuts the spinal cord in the middle of the back. Which signals are affected?

options.text: Only the signals from the brain to the legs
Impulses between the brain and the body below the injury, in both directions
Only the sensations from the legs to the brain
None, since the brain controls the whole body directly

image.alt: Side view of the backbone with a damaged spinal cord; impulses from below and commands from the brain are blocked at the injury

hint: The spinal cord carries messages both up and down.
explanation: The spinal cord carries sensory impulses **up to the brain** and motor commands **down from the brain**. A cut blocks both ways below the injury. The brain cannot reach muscles directly; it needs the cord and nerves, so the other options are incomplete or wrong.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Side view of the human brain showing the fore-brain, mid-brain, cerebellum, medulla and the start of the spinal cord

assertion: The medulla controls salivation and vomiting.
reason: The medulla is a part of the hind-brain.
hint: Is the fact in R the reason for A?
explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. The medulla controls these involuntary actions because of its connections and role, not simply because it is in the hind-brain (the cerebellum is also in the hind-brain but does a different job).

subject: biology
prompt: The leaves of a sensitive plant fold when touched. This movement is

options.text: independent of growth
caused by growth of the leaf stalk
controlled by muscles in the leaf
controlled by a nervous system in the stem

image.alt: A sensitive plant: touching a leaf makes the leaflets fold and the leaf stalks droop within seconds

hint: The leaves move within seconds.
explanation: The sensitive plant's leaf movement is **quick and not related to growth**. Plants have neither muscles nor nerves; the information is passed from cell to cell by electrical-chemical means. Directional growth movements (like a seedling) are slow and depend on growth.

subject: biology
prompt: How do cells in a sensitive plant change shape so that the leaf droops?

options.text: Special muscle proteins shorten the cells
Cells divide rapidly on one side
By changing the amount of water in them, so they swell or shrink
They secrete auxin on the shady side

image.alt: Before touch the cells at the base of a sensitive plant leaf are swollen with water; after touch water leaves, the cells shrink and the leaf droops

hint: Plants have no muscle proteins.
explanation: Plant cells change shape by **gaining or losing water**: swelling or shrinking. Special proteins are what animal muscle cells use, cell division is a growth process, and auxin is linked to growth movements, not the quick touch response.

subject: biology
prompt: A pea tendril coils around a support because

options.text: the part in contact grows faster than the far side
the part in contact with the support grows more slowly than the part away from it
the tendril has muscles that contract
the tendril shrinks in the light

image.alt: A pea tendril coiling round a support because the side touching it grows more slowly than the far side

hint: Think about which side is longer when a tendril curls.
explanation: When the tendril touches a support, the side in contact **grows less rapidly** than the far side. The faster-growing outer side makes the tendril circle round and cling to the support. This is a growth movement, not muscle action.

subject: biology
prompt: In Activity 6.2, bean seedlings are kept in a box for a few days. The box is open towards a window on the **right**. Which picture shows the result?

options.text: Shoot and root both bend right

image.alt: Shoot and root both bend right, towards the light

options.text: Shoot bends right towards the light and root bends left, away from it

image.alt: Shoot bends right towards the light and root bends left, away from it

options.text: Shoot bends left and root bends right

image.alt: Shoot bends left away from the light and root bends right

options.text: Shoot and root both stay straight

image.alt: Shoot and root both grow straight
Bean seedlings on a flask inside a box open towards a window: shoots bend towards the light and roots bend away from it

hint: Shoots go towards light, roots away.
explanation: Shoots show **positive phototropism** (bend towards light) and roots bend **away** from it. Turning the flask later changes only the direction of **new growth**; old parts keep their bend.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the place where the plant hormone **auxin** is **synthesised** (made).

image.alt: A shoot with light shining from the right; auxin made at the tip moves down the shaded left side where cells grow longer

spots.label: Shaded side (auxin gathers, cells grow longer)

hint: It is made where growth is directed from.
explanation: Auxin is synthesised at the **shoot tip**. When light comes from one side, it diffuses down towards the shady side.

subject: biology
prompt: Light falls on a shoot from the right. Which picture shows how **auxin** is distributed (spread)?

options.text: Auxin gathered on the right, lit side

image.alt: Auxin dots gathered on the right side, facing the light

options.text: Auxin spread evenly on both sides

image.alt: Auxin dots spread evenly on both sides

options.text: Auxin gathered on the left, shaded side

image.alt: Auxin dots gathered on the left, shaded side of the shoot

options.text: Auxin only at the very tip

image.alt: Auxin dots only at the very tip
A shoot with light shining from the right; auxin made at the tip moves down the shaded left side where cells grow longer

hint: Auxin moves away from light.
explanation: Auxin diffuses towards the **shady side**, making cells there grow **longer**, so the shoot bends towards the light. If auxin stayed even or gathered on the lit side, the shoot would not bend towards the light.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the events that make a shoot **bend towards light**.

image.alt: A shoot with light shining from the right; auxin made at the tip moves down the shaded left side where cells grow longer

items.text: The higher auxin concentration stimulates the shady-side cells to grow longer
Light falls on the growing shoot from one side
The shady side becomes longer than the side facing the light
Auxin from the shoot tip diffuses towards the shady side
The shoot appears to bend towards the light

hint: Auxin goes to the shady side, then growth, then bending.
explanation: When light comes from one side, auxin (synthesised at the shoot tip) diffuses towards the **shady side**. This concentration stimulates those cells to grow longer, so the shady side becomes longer and the shoot **appears to bend towards light**.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A shoot with light shining from the right; auxin made at the tip moves down the shaded left side where cells grow longer

assertion: Auxin makes the cells on the side of the shoot facing the light grow longer.
reason: Auxin diffuses towards the shady side of the shoot.
hint: On which side does auxin gather?
explanation: A is false: auxin makes cells on the **shady** side grow longer. R is true: auxin diffuses towards the shady side. That causes the shoot to bend towards light.

subject: biology
prompt: Shoots grow upwards and roots grow downwards in response to the pull of the earth. This movement is called

options.text: phototropism
hydrotropism
chemotropism
geotropism

image.alt: A germinating seed with the root growing down towards gravity and the shoot growing upwards

hint: 'Geo' refers to the earth.
explanation: **Geotropism** is directional growth in response to **gravity**. Phototropism is to light, hydrotropism to water and chemotropism to chemicals (for example pollen tubes growing towards ovules).

subject: biology
prompt: A root grows sideways through the soil towards a patch of damp soil. Which picture shows this **hydrotropism**?

options.text: Root curving towards the wet soil

image.alt: Root curving towards the wet soil on the right

options.text: Root curving away from the wet soil

image.alt: Root curving away from the wet soil, to the left

options.text: Root growing straight down

image.alt: Root growing straight down

options.text: Root curling back upwards

image.alt: Root curling back upwards
A root growing sideways through soil towards a patch of wet soil

hint: Hydro means water, tropism means growth movement.
explanation: In **hydrotropism** roots grow towards water. The root bends towards the wet patch.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each directional growth movement with its stimulus (what it responds to).

image.alt: A germinating seed with the root growing down towards gravity and the shoot growing upwards
Shoot bends right towards the light and root bends left, away from it
A germinating seed with the root growing down towards gravity and the shoot growing upwards
Root curving towards the wet soil on the right
A pollen tube growing down the style towards the ovule, guided by chemicals released by the ovule

hint: Hydro = water, chemo = chemicals.
explanation: Phototropism responds to **light**, geotropism to **gravity**, hydrotropism to **water**, chemotropism to **chemicals**, for example pollen tubes growing towards ovules.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange these plant movements from the **fastest** to the **slowest**.

image.alt: A sensitive plant: touching a leaf makes the leaflets fold and the leaf stalks droop within seconds

items.text: Shoot bends towards light over several days

image.alt: Shoot bends right towards the light and root bends left, away from it

items.text: Sensitive plant folds its leaves on touch

image.alt: A sensitive plant: touching a leaf makes the leaflets fold and the leaf stalks droop within seconds

items.text: Sunflower moves in response to day or night

image.alt: A sunflower head slowly turning to follow the sun across the sky from morning to evening

hint: Touch response needs no growth.
explanation: The sensitive plant responds to touch very quickly, the movement of sunflowers in response to day or night is quite slow, and growth-related movement such as a shoot bending towards light is even slower.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these plant hormones help in **promoting growth**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A short stem next to a tall stem that has grown longer under the effect of gibberellins

options.text: Auxin
Gibberellins
Cytokinins
Abscisic acid
Insulin

hint: Abscisic acid is the one that stops growth.
explanation: **Auxin** and **gibberellins** help the stem grow and **cytokinins** promote cell division. **Abscisic acid** inhibits growth (causing wilting of leaves). **Insulin** is an animal hormone.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each plant hormone with its effect.

image.alt: A potted plant showing growing shoot tip, lengthening stem, a fruit with seeds and a drooping leaf

right.text: Like auxins, help in the growth of the stem
Diffuses to the shady side of a shoot, making those cells grow longer

hint: Cytokinesis means cell division.
explanation: **Auxin** lengthens cells, **gibberellins** help stem growth, **cytokinins** promote cell division (high in fruits and seeds), and **abscisic acid** inhibits growth.

subject: biology
prompt: One plant hormone **inhibits growth** (stops or slows growth). Its effects include wilting of leaves. Which hormone is it?

options.text: Auxin
Abscisic acid
Gibberellin
Cytokinin

image.alt: A healthy plant beside a plant whose leaves droop and wilt under abscisic acid, a growth inhibitor

hint: Plants also need a signal to stop growing.
explanation: **Abscisic acid** stops growth and is linked to wilting. Auxin, gibberellins and cytokinins promote growth.

subject: biology
prompt: Cytokinins are present in higher amounts in areas of rapid cell division, such as

options.text: fruits and seeds
mature leaves only
dead bark
root caps only

image.alt: Cells dividing again and again in a fruit with seeds, where cytokinins are most concentrated

hint: Rapid cell division is common in young fruits and seeds.
explanation: Cytokinins **promote cell division**, so they are more concentrated where cells divide rapidly, such as in **fruits and seeds**.

subject: biology
prompt: Most multicellular organisms use **chemical communication** as well as electrical impulses. Why?

options.text: Electrical impulses are slower than chemicals
Hormones need nerve tissue to reach every cell
Electrical impulses reach only connected cells and a cell needs time to reset before sending a new impulse, whereas hormones can reach all cells steadily
Cells can send electrical impulses continuously without rest

image.alt: A nerve impulse racing along a nerve to one connected cell compared with hormone molecules slowly spreading to many cells

hint: Think of two limitations of electrical impulses.
explanation: Electrical impulses are an excellent fast means, but (1) they reach only cells **connected by nervous tissue** and (2) a cell needs time to **reset** before another impulse. Chemical signals diffuse to all cells and can act steadily and persistently, although slower.

subject: biology
prompt: Which statements about **hormonal (chemical) coordination** are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A nerve impulse racing along a nerve to one connected cell compared with hormone molecules slowly spreading to many cells

options.text: It is slower than nerve impulses
It can reach all cells of the body
It can be steady and persistent
It needs nerve connections to every cell
It uses electrical impulses

hint: Hormones travel by diffusion or blood.
explanation: Hormones are slower but can reach **every cell** and work steadily. They do not need nerves to every cell and they are chemical, not electrical.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A nerve impulse racing along a nerve to one connected cell compared with hormone molecules slowly spreading to many cells

assertion: Nervous coordination is faster than hormonal coordination.
reason: Electrical impulses can reach each and every cell of the animal body.
hint: Do impulses reach cells without nerve connections?
explanation: A is true: impulses travel quickly. R is false: impulses reach only cells **connected by nervous tissue**. Hormones can reach every cell.

subject: biology
prompt: A squirrel is scared. Why is a **chemical signal** (adrenaline) more useful here than only nerve impulses?

options.text: It reaches all cells of the body, bringing the wide-ranging changes needed for either fighting or running
Nerves cannot carry any signals in an emergency
It works much faster than nerve impulses
It only affects the brain

image.alt: A frightened squirrel facing a growling dog must either run away or fight, so its body prepares for both

hint: Both fighting and running need many tissues to prepare.
explanation: Nerve impulses would reach only a limited set of tissues. **Adrenaline**, secreted into the blood, reaches many tissues and prepares the body for both running and fighting. It is not faster than nerves and it does not act only on the brain.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the gland that secretes **adrenaline**.

image.alt: A human body outline with the pituitary in the head, thyroid in the neck, adrenal glands above the kidneys, pancreas and ovaries

hint: It sits just above the kidneys.
explanation: The **adrenal glands**, above the kidneys, secrete adrenaline directly into the blood.

subject: biology
prompt: **Adrenaline** is secreted (released) into the blood. Which of these are responses to it? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Adrenaline from the adrenal gland travels in the blood: the heart beats faster, more blood goes to the muscles and less to the gut and skin

options.text: The heart beats faster
Breathing rate increases
Blood flow to the digestive system and skin decreases
Blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles
Blood flow to the digestive system increases

hint: Adrenaline gets the body ready for action.
explanation: Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster, increases breathing, narrows arteries to digestive system and skin, and diverts blood to skeletal muscles. More blood to the gut is the opposite.

subject: biology
prompt: How does adrenaline reduce blood flow to the digestive system and skin?

options.text: The heart stops pumping blood there
Muscles around small arteries in those organs contract
The blood vessels burst
Hormones are not released there

image.alt: Adrenaline from the adrenal gland travels in the blood: the heart beats faster, more blood goes to the muscles and less to the gut and skin

hint: Contraction narrows a tube.
explanation: Contraction of muscles around small arteries in these organs narrows them, diverting blood to the **skeletal muscles**.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **thyroid gland**. It needs iodine to make thyroxin.

image.alt: A human body outline with the pituitary in the head, thyroid in the neck, adrenal glands above the kidneys, pancreas and ovaries

hint: It lies in the neck.
explanation: The **thyroid gland** is in the neck. A swollen neck (goitre) is a symptom of iodine deficiency.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each deficiency or problem with the condition it causes.

image.alt: A feedback loop: rising blood sugar makes the pancreas release more insulin, sugar falls, and insulin release is reduced
A person with a swollen neck
A very short adult standing next to an average-height person
A drop of blood loaded with sugar cubes next to an insulin syringe

hint: Match iodine to thyroid, growth hormone to height.
explanation: Iodine is needed for thyroxin, so deficiency can cause **goitre**; lack of **growth hormone** in childhood causes **dwarfism**; insufficient **insulin** raises blood sugar, as in **diabetes**.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Iodine from iodised salt feeds the thyroid gland; a normal thyroid beside a swollen thyroid causing goitre

assertion: We are advised to use iodised salt in our diet.
reason: Iodine is essential for the thyroid gland to make thyroxin.
hint: What does thyroxin need?
explanation: Both true and R explains A. Iodine deficiency can cause goitre (swollen neck).

subject: biology
prompt: A child has a deficiency (shortage) of **growth hormone**. Which condition does this lead to? Choose the picture.

options.text: A very short adult (dwarfism)

image.alt: A very short adult standing next to an average-height person

options.text: An extremely tall person (giant)

image.alt: An extremely tall person standing next to an average-height person

options.text: A swollen neck (goitre)

image.alt: A person with a swollen neck

options.text: Two people of the same height (normal)

image.alt: Two people of the same average height
A human body outline with the pituitary in the head, thyroid in the neck, adrenal glands above the kidneys, pancreas and ovaries

hint: Growth hormone comes from the pituitary.
explanation: Growth hormone is secreted by the **pituitary**. Deficiency in childhood leads to **dwarfism**.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each hormone with the gland that produces it.

image.alt: A human body outline with the pituitary in the head, thyroid in the neck, adrenal glands above the kidneys, pancreas and ovaries

hint: Think of the position of the gland.
explanation: **Insulin** is made by the pancreas, **thyroxin** by the thyroid, **adrenaline** by the adrenal glands and **testosterone** by the testes.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the **feedback** events that control blood sugar.

image.alt: A feedback loop: rising blood sugar makes the pancreas release more insulin, sugar falls, and insulin release is reduced

items.text: Pancreas releases more insulin
Blood sugar level rises
Blood sugar level falls
Cells of the pancreas detect the rise
Insulin secretion is reduced

hint: Detect, respond, fall, reduce.
explanation: A rise in blood sugar is detected by pancreas cells, which produce **more insulin**. As sugar falls, insulin secretion is **reduced**. This is a feedback mechanism.
